title: What did she say? — reported speech and polite requests
goal: Pass on what someone said or asked (*katanya, bilang, bahwa, apakah*) and make requests at the right level of politeness (*tolong, mohon, silakan, coba, minta*) — from a colleague's desk to the immigration counter.
bekal: pass on a message: *Pak Hendra bilang bahwa beliau senang*, *Beliau tanya apakah kita sudah siap*
ask, invite and instruct politely: *Tolong fotokopi…*, *Silakan duduk*, *Mohon ditunggu*

notes: **Beliau** is the respectful "he/she" for someone senior or older: your boss, a teacher, a grandmother, the President. Bayu would never call Pak Hendra *dia* in this context. Note that *beliau* is only for third persons — you cannot address someone as *beliau*.

**Katanya — "he says, she said".** *Kata* is "word", so *katanya* is "his word": the everyday way to report what someone said without naming the verb. With a name it becomes *kata* + person: *Kata Rina, …*, *Kata beliau, …* (according to Rina, according to him).

**Bilang and bahwa.** *Bilang* 💬 is the everyday "say, tell"; the written verbs are *berkata* and *mengatakan*. *Bahwa* is "that" and is optional in speech — *Beliau bilang kantor pusat senang* is just as good. In a report or email, keep *bahwa*.

**Apakah — "whether".** Yes/no questions are reported with *apakah*: *Beliau tanya apakah kita sudah siap*. Question-word questions just keep their question word: *Beliau tanya kapan videonya jadi.* And the tense never shifts: "are we ready" stays *sudah siap*.

**Titip salam — "send regards".** *Titip* is to leave something in someone's care, and a greeting is something you can entrust to a messenger: *Titip salam buat Bu Endang, ya.* The polite reply is *Salam balik* (regards back) or *Nanti saya sampaikan* (I'll pass it on).

**Yang penting — "the main thing is".** It closes discussions all over Indonesia: *Yang penting sehat* (what matters is being healthy), *Yang penting sampai* (as long as we get there). **Paling lambat** is "at the latest" (*lambat*, slow); its opposite is *paling cepat*, "at the earliest".

grammars.title: Passing it on
body: To report speech, change the pronouns and keep everything else. Indonesian has no tense change and no word-order change in reported questions.

You report
English

He asked when the video would be done.
He asked you to prepare a video.
He asked us not to be late.

after: Requests are reported with *minta* (ask for, ask to) and orders with *suruh* (tell to): *Ibu menyuruh Dimas mandi* (his mother told Dimas to have a bath).
💬 In speech many people say *kalau* where writing needs *bahwa* or *apakah*: *Dia bilang kalau dia capek*, *Coba tanya kalau dia bisa*. Understand it; write *bahwa* and *apakah*.

grammars.title: The many faces of katanya
body: *Katanya* is a small word with a big range, from a plain report to open scepticism. Tone and context tell you which.

after: Because *katanya* can hint at doubt, use *kata beliau* or *beliau bilang* when passing on your boss's words. *Katanya Pak Hendra puas* can sound as if you are not quite convinced he is.

notes: **Ibu for Sarah.** At a government counter Sarah is *Ibu* (madam), not *Mbak*: *Apakah Ibu membawa…?* Officials address the public with *Bapak/Ibu*, and it is used instead of "you". Answer with *Pak* and *saya* and you are matching register perfectly.

**Silakan** invites someone to do something that benefits **them**: *Silakan duduk* (do sit down), *Silakan masuk* (come in). Sarah's *Silakan, Pak* means "go ahead" — she is granting permission for him to check. ⚠️ Never say *silakan* when you want someone to do something for **you**; that is *tolong*.

**Tolong** asks for a favour or gives a polite instruction: *Tolong fotokopi halaman identitas.* It is "please" in the sense of "help me by…". Officials use it too, which makes an instruction sound like a request.

**Mohon + di- verb** is the formal request of institutions: *Mohon ditunggu* ("it is requested that [this] be waited for" — please wait), *Mohon pastikan…* (please ensure…). The passive keeps it impersonal, which is exactly what an office wants.

**KITAS** (*Kartu Izin Tinggal Terbatas*) is the limited stay permit for foreign residents. Procedures change often and much of it is now online, so always check the official immigration website before you go; the photo and fingerprint appointment, however, is still in person.

**Loket, koperasi, sidik jari.** *Loket* is a service counter or ticket window. A *koperasi* (co-operative) in a government office is the staff shop, and it always has a photocopier. *Sidik jari* (fingerprint) is literally "finger trace".

grammars.title: Asking nicely: the request toolkit
body: English uses "please" for all of these. Indonesian chooses by who benefits and how formal the situation is.
after: *Minta tolong* combines the two: *Boleh minta tolong?* (could I ask you a favour?) is the perfect opener before any request to a stranger.

blocks.text: In conversation *bilang*, *tanya* and *minta* do almost everything. In writing — emails, minutes, reports — you need the full *me-* and *ber-* verbs.
Note *menanyakan* (ask about something, with an object) against *bertanya* (ask, no object): *Dia bertanya kepada saya* but *Dia menanyakan harga tiketnya*.
When someone rings for a colleague who is out, this is the exchange. Notice how much of it uses *beliau* and passive-style requests.
